SECTION 010:00–4:26

More unknowns than equations force a nonzero nullspace

A wide homogeneous system always has a free variable.

This lecture gives precise meanings to four connected ideas: linear independence, span, basis, and dimension. Strang starts with a fact supplied by elimination.

Let A have m rows and n columns, with more unknowns than equations: n > m. If its rank is r, there are at most m pivots, so

r ≤ m < n,   n − r ≥ n − m > 0.

There is at least one free variable. Give one free variable the value 1, set the other free variables to 0, and solve the pivot equations. This produces a special solution of Ax = 0 that is nonzero, because its chosen free coordinate is 1.

The homogeneous system is always consistent. Its zero solution is guaranteed, and the free variable guarantees additional solutions. This counting argument will explain why too many vectors in a space must be dependent.

The opening fact

More columns than rows guarantees a nonzero solution of Ax = 0. There are at least n − m free variables.

SECTION 024:26–7:05

Independence means only the zero combination gives zero

The coefficients must all vanish, not merely their sum.

A list of vectors v₁, …, vₙ is linearly independent when the equation

c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ··· + cₙvₙ = 0

has only the coefficient choice c₁ = ··· = cₙ = 0. This is the zero combination. It always gives the zero vector; independence says it is the only combination that does.

The vectors are dependent if some coefficient choice, with at least one coefficient nonzero, also produces the zero vector. Some coefficients may still be zero. “Nonzero combination” refers to the coefficient list, even though its resulting vector is zero.

A dependence relation can be rearranged to express one vector as a combination of the others: solve for any vector whose coefficient is nonzero. Such a vector adds no new direction to the span.

Equivalent interpretation. Rearranging a nontrivial relation makes the lecture’s direct meaning of dependence explicit. Independence is a property of the listed vectors; a matrix provides a way to test its columns.

SECTION 037:05–10:00

Multiples and the zero vector give immediate dependence

One nontrivial zero combination is enough to settle the question.

If v₂ = 2v₁, the two vectors are dependent. Their relation is

2v₁ − v₂ = 0.

The coefficients (2, −1) are not both zero. Geometrically the two arrows lie along the same line, so the second adds no new direction.

Now take v₁ = (2, 1)ᵀ and v₂ = (0, 0)ᵀ. A relation is even easier:

0[21]+6[00]=[00]

The first coefficient is zero, but the second is 6. This is a nontrivial relation, so the list is dependent.

Any list containing the zero vector is dependent: put coefficient 1 on that vector and 0 on every other vector. No information about the remaining vectors is needed.

SECTION 0410:00–13:19

Three vectors in the plane must be dependent

Put the vectors into a two-by-three matrix and apply the opening fact.

Two nonparallel nonzero vectors in R² are independent. Adding a third vector creates dependence, regardless of how its arrow is drawn. Put the three vectors into the columns of a matrix:

P=[215/212−1]

The coefficient equation Pc = 0 has two equations and three unknowns. The opening pivot-count argument guarantees a nonzero coefficient vector, so the columns are dependent.

For the coordinates Strang suggests, one exact relation is

−4v₁ + 3v₂ + 2v₃ = 0,
equivalently v₃ = 2v₁ − (3/2)v₂.

Check the two components: −8 + 3 + 5 = 0 and −4 + 6 − 2 = 0. The relation identifies how the third arrow is built from the first two.

Sketch versus calculation. The lecture chooses these coordinates informally from the drawing. The numerical relation is completed here; the general conclusion holds for any three vectors in R².

SECTION 0513:19–18:06

Test column independence through the nullspace

Independent columns mean every column is a pivot column.

For vectors v₁, …, vₙ in Rᵐ, form A = [v₁ ··· vₙ]. Multiplying by a coefficient vector packages the linear combination:

Ac = c₁v₁ + ··· + cₙvₙ.

The vectors are independent precisely when Ac = 0 has only c = 0. In the language developed in the last two lectures, the following statements are equivalent:

NULLSPACE

N(A) = {0}

No nonzero coefficient vector gives zero.

PIVOTS

r = n

Every column has a pivot.

VARIABLES

No free variables

The homogeneous solution has no freedom.

If r < n, a free variable produces a nonzero special solution. Its entries are the coefficients of a dependence relation among A’s columns.

The nullspace always contains the zero vector. When the lecture asks whether there is “something in the null space,” the relevant test is whether there is anything other than zero.

Elimination preserves the solutions of Ac = 0. It therefore detects dependencies among the original columns, even though the row operations change the actual column vectors.

SECTION 0618:06–21:52

The span contains all linear combinations

A spanning list reaches every vector in the specified space.

The span of v₁, …, vₖ is the set of all their linear combinations:

span{v₁, …, vₖ} = {c₁v₁ + ··· + cₖvₖ : c₁, …, cₖ ∈ R}.

The vectors span a space S when this set equals S. Every vector of S must be obtainable. The target matters: a list may span a plane inside R³ without spanning all of R³.

The span is the smallest subspace containing the given vectors. Any subspace containing them must contain all their combinations. Conversely, the combinations themselves form a subspace: they contain zero and remain combinations after addition or scalar multiplication.

The columns of A always span C(A), by the definition of column space. They may be dependent or independent; spanning alone does not decide that question.

Two separate tests

Independence asks whether a nontrivial combination gives zero. Spanning asks whether all vectors in the target space can be reached.

SECTION 0721:52–26:41

A basis is independent and spans the space

The coordinate vectors give the standard basis for R³.

A basis for a vector space S is a list of vectors in S with two properties: the vectors are linearly independent, and they span S.

Spanning guarantees enough vectors to describe the whole space. Independence removes redundancy. The list is “just right” in both senses.

The standard example for R³ is

e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001]

A combination c₁e₁ + c₂e₂ + c₃e₃ is the vector (c₁, c₂, c₃)ᵀ. It equals zero only if all three coefficients vanish, and it reaches every vector in R³ by choosing its three components as coefficients.

Putting these vectors into columns gives I₃. The identity has three pivots and no nonzero nullspace vectors.

Unique coordinates. A basis represents every vector in exactly one way. Spanning gives existence. If two coefficient lists represented the same vector, subtracting them would give a zero combination; independence forces their difference to be zero.

SECTION 0826:41–30:46

Check a proposed basis instead of trusting its appearance

For n vectors in Rⁿ, the column matrix must be invertible.

Strang starts another example with u = (1, 1, 2)ᵀ and v = (2, 2, 5)ᵀ. They are independent: v is not twice u, because 5 is not 4. But two vectors do not span R³.

Adding (3, 3, 7)ᵀ does not help, because that vector is u + v. The lecture then proposes w = (3, 3, 8)ᵀ and suggests the three might be a basis.

Correction to the proposed basis. The vector (3, 3, 8) is not u + v, but it is still a combination: w = −u + 2v. All three have equal first and second components, so they remain in the plane x = y. The original spoken claim and board entries are retained in the transcript and reference image; the study calculation corrects the claim.
M=[123123258]

The first two rows coincide. Row reduction gives only two pivots, and the relation u − 2v + w = 0 proves dependence directly.

The lecture also mentions z = (5, 7, −14)ᵀ as another candidate. This one lies outside x = y and really does extend u and v to a basis:

G=[12512725−14]

Its reduced form is I₃. To see the third pivot directly, subtract row 1 from row 2 and twice row 1 from row 3. The lower rows become (0, 0, 2) and (0, 1, −24); swap them to see three nonzero pivots.

In general, n vectors form a basis for Rⁿ exactly when the n × n matrix with those columns is invertible. Merely being different vectors, or avoiding one particular sum, is not enough.

SECTION 0930:46–32:36

The same two vectors are a basis for their plane

Always name the space whose basis is being requested.

The pair u, v fails to be a basis for R³, but it is a basis for the subspace it spans. Its combinations are

αu + βv = (α + 2β, α + 2β, 2α + 5β)ᵀ.

These vectors have equal first and second components. Conversely, any (t, t, s)ᵀ is obtained by taking

β = s − 2t,   α = 5t − 2s.

Thus the span is exactly the plane S = {(t, t, s)ᵀ : t, s ∈ R}, or x = y. Since u and v are independent, they form a basis for S.

Adding u + v gives three vectors that still span S. They are no longer a basis, because the extra vector is redundant.

Plane identified explicitly. The lecture describes the span as a plane. Its equation and the coefficient formulas above are editorial checks for the displayed entries. The drawing is a projection of that infinite plane.

SECTION 1032:36–37:44

Every basis has the same number of vectors

That common number is the dimension of the space.

A space usually has many different bases. The standard coordinate vectors form one basis of R³, and the columns of any invertible three-by-three matrix form another.

The central theorem is that every basis for a given finite-dimensional space contains the same number of vectors. This common number is the dimension:

dim S = number of vectors in any basis for S.

So dim R³ = 3 and dim Rⁿ = n. The plane x = y has dimension 2, even though its vectors each have three components.

Why cannot a second basis have more vectors? Suppose a basis has d vectors. Express k other vectors in its coordinates, making a d × k coefficient matrix. If k > d, the opening wide-system fact gives a nontrivial zero combination of those coefficient columns, hence a dependence among the k vectors. An independent list therefore has at most d vectors. Applying this to two bases in both directions forces their sizes to agree.

The theorem’s reason. The lecture states the equal-size theorem. The coordinate-matrix argument above supplies a short justification using its opening fact.

In a space of dimension d, more than d vectors cannot be independent, and fewer than d cannot span the space. With exactly d vectors in S, independence or spanning alone is enough to establish a basis.

Its four columns span C(A), as matrix columns always do. They are dependent because

The natural choice is columns 1 and 2: a₁ = (1, 1, 1)ᵀ and a₂ = (2, 1, 2)ᵀ. They are not multiples, and columns 3 and 4 are combinations of them. Thus {a₁, a₂} is a basis for C(A).

SECTION 1241:06–43:25

Rank is the dimension of the column space

A matrix has a rank; a vector space has a dimension.

The pivot columns are independent, and the free columns are combinations of pivot columns. The original pivot columns therefore form a basis for the original column space.

There are r pivot columns, so the basis contains r vectors:

rank(A) = r = dim C(A).

For this three-by-four example, rank(A) = 2 and dim C(A) = 2. All its columns have first and third components equal. Since the first two independent columns span a plane,

C(A) = {(t, s, t)ᵀ : t, s ∈ R}.

This plane is x = z. It differs from the earlier plane x = y; the examples use different vector lists.

The matrix has three rows and four columns. Those describe its shape. Its column space is a two-dimensional subspace of R³. Strang emphasizes this language because it keeps the object and its associated space distinct.

SECTION 1446:09–49:58

Special solutions form a nullspace basis

The number of free variables is the nullspace dimension.

The column relations already gave one nullspace vector. The duplicate fourth column gives another. With the free coordinates x₃ and x₄ chosen as (1, 0) and (0, 1), the special solutions are

s1=[−1−110],s2=[−1001]

Both satisfy As = 0. They are independent because their free-coordinate pairs are (1, 0) and (0, 1): a zero combination must give coefficient zero on each.

They also span the entire nullspace. The reduced equations are x₁ + x₃ + x₄ = 0 and x₂ + x₃ = 0. Letting x₃ = c and x₄ = d gives every homogeneous solution:

x = (−c − d, −c, c, d)ᵀ = cs₁ + ds₂.

Thus {s₁, s₂} is a basis for N(A), and dim N(A) = 2. These vectors live in R⁴, while the column-space basis vectors live in R³. The two spaces happen to have the same dimension in this example.

For a general m × n matrix of rank r, each of the n − r free variables supplies one independent special solution. Their combinations give every homogeneous solution, so

dim C(A) = r,   dim N(A) = n − r,
dim C(A) + dim N(A) = n.
Four words, one computation

Elimination identifies the pivot columns and free variables. They provide bases for the column space and nullspace, whose sizes give their dimensions.

Spanning made explicit. The lecture states that the two special solutions are a nullspace basis. The full parameterization above verifies that they span every solution.
